subsubtopic: NEED FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION TO MAKE JACQUES CARTIER BRIDGE SAFE IN MONTREAL
speechtext:
Two weeks ago, Mr. Speaker, Montreal's Jacques Cartier Bridge was again the scene of serious accidents, including one which resulted in the death of a Montreal south shore woman resident. It so happens that for several months now the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) has had on his desk the Trafix consultant firm report recommending quite realistic and practicable measures to make that bridge safer.
We Liberal Members of the Montreal region wonder just how much longer it will take before the Conservative Government reacts, just how much time before the Minister of Transport realizes the seriousness of the situation and heeds the advice of the Ports Canada Police Fraternity and of his own advisers who are urging him to take action. He has to assume his responsibilities before more accidents occur.

subsubtopic: IMPORTANCE OF FOREST INDUSTRY TO ECONOMY OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you well know, in British Columbia money really does grow on trees. Over $1 billion annually is generated in taxes and direct revenues from B.C.'s forest industry.
Today is day six of National Forest Week in Canada. As a Member of Parliament representing a forest riding, including Port Alberni, the Forestry Capital of Canada, this week is especially meaningful to the citizens of my home province. This year close to 90 British Columbia communities are joining with other communities across Canada to recognize our
most valuable natural resource through community events, fairs and other festivities.
Much like the people of British Columbia, the forests of our province are undoubtedly one of the nation's greatest assets. One out of every three jobs in British Columbia depends on the forest resource for their livelihood. Ten per cent of our national economy is fueled by our forests.
Clearly money does grow on trees. Today, during National Forest Week, we recognize the contribution our forests make to the lives of all Canadians.

subsubtopic: ACCIDENTAL DEATH OF VANCOUVER TEENAGER AT SELFSERVICE GAS STATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have before me the coroner's report on the death of Edward Siemens, a Vancouver teenager who was a very great athlete. He and three other teenagers had been travelling in Vancouver late at night. They ran out of gas and manoeuvred their car into a self-service gas station.
The report indicates the power steering was very stiff and they were having difficulty manoeuvring the vehicle past the gas pumps. The right front of the vehicle impacted the gas pump and somehow the hose of number two pump caught the bumper of the car ripping the hose from the pump and breaking the on-off lever. This sudden disruption then caused the gas to be dispensed uncontrollably on to the ground surrounding the gas pump island area.
Mr. Siemens got out of the car. The electrical spark was still on, a fire broke out and engulfed Edward Siemens, and he died.
The report has a lot of good recommendations including larger islands, proper signage, fire extinguishers, two-way intercoms, proper training procedures, electrical shut-off switches and so on, but I want to bring to the attention of the House one particular recommendation, and I quote:
We recommend a public awareness program as to the dangers of gasoline at
self-service gas stations. This program should be province-wide.
I think it should be Canada-wide. I hope we can learn from Edward Siemens' death so we can prevent this kind of tragic death of another teenager or anyone else.

May 8, 1987

subsubtopic: WORLD WAR II-ANNIVERSARY OF VICTORY DAY, MAY 8, 1945
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after five years, World War II came to a slow and grinding halt. My war between Nijmegen and Arnhem was literally bogged down. It was on April 27, while on brigade staff, that I delivered the message: "Fire only when fired upon".
On May 5 General Foulkes accepted the surrender of the German forces in Holland. The lights went up. There were no more black-outs. We shook hands. We were still alive.
On May 7, in a brief ceremony at Reimes, General Jodi signed the surrender document, with hostilities to cease the next day. Thus, World War II ended on May 8, 1945.
Canadians will be forever remembered in the Netherlands with these words: "Thank you, Canada, for giving us our freedom".
Canadians lie buried in 74 different countries. May 8, 1945, was Victory Day-freedom so bitterly won.

subsubtopic: COUNTERVAIL IMPOSED ON IMPORTS OF UNITED STATES CORN-FUNDING OF ACTION BY AMERICAN FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Ontario corn producers are suffering tremendous uncertainty as a result of the latest move by the United States to fight the countervail which Canada recently imposed on highly subsidized U.S. corn. The 85 cents per bushel countervail assists Canadian farmers by imposing a price on U.S. corn which is more in line with Canadian prices. The effect of the U.S. Farm Bill has been to depress corn prices severely and artificially thereby unfairly hurting our corn producers. This action by Canada was necessary.
The latest U.S. proposal would provide by law $500,000 to American farm groups who want to fight against the fair and necessary 85-cent Canadian countervail on corn. Whereas Canadian corn producers have paid their own legal bills, we see in this case the real possibility that the United States Treasury will be pitted against the already hurting Canadian corn producers. This U.S. financial assistance to farmers is in itself another subsidy to U.S. producers who are already among the most highly subsidized in the world.
I call upon the Government to protest this action immediately and do whatever it can to block such an unfair U.S. plan.

Mr. Speaker, while there are some encouraging signs in today's employment figures, the jobless situation in most of Canada remains at an excessively high and totally unacceptable level.
The jobless figure for central British Columbia is 4 per cent higher than it was a year ago, while the jobless numbers for young people remain at virtually immorally high levels.
Youth unemployment in British Columbia has increased by 157 per cent during the 1980s, yet the Government has only provided summer job funds equal to those of last year. With no Expo jobs this summer, the job prospects for students and other young people in British Columbia will obviously be worse.
The federal Government has refused to recognize this critical fact in its funding for Challenge '87. While the Government points out that more than 90 per cent of all new jobs in Canada occur in the greater Toronto area, it should recognize that there is a Canada beyond Toronto in southern Ontario.
The unemployment crisis is continuing in all regions of Canada and is even increasing in the Province of Newfoundland. It is time the Government acknowledged this human tragedy and took immediate steps to bring it to an end.

subsubtopic: PROJECT LAY-OFFS IN MARITIME LUMBER MILLS
speechtext:

subsubtopic: ACCESS BY CANADIAN ASTRONOMERS TO NEW TELESCOPE IN HAWAII
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, through a collaborative agreement signed recently between the National Research Council and Britain's Scientific and Engineering Research Council, Canadian astronomers will have access to 25 per cent of the observing time on one of world's best ratio telescopes operating at sub-millimetric wavelengths, a previously inaccessible spectral window on the universe.
This facility, the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope, will start operating this June on the 4,300 metre high summit of Mount Mauna Kea in Hawaii. Mauna Kea is one of the world's best astronomical sites because of its very dry atmosphere and the absence of light pollution. For this reason, a growing number of major telescopes operate there at visible, infrared and millimetric wavelengths, including the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope, a world class facility used by Canadian astronomers working in the visible part of the spectrum.
The National Research Council will also give Canadian astronomers convenient access to the new frontier in astronomy, the unprecedented resolution and spectral coverage of the Hubble Space Telescope. Located far above the earth's atmosphere, the Space Telescope will provide opportunities for dramatic new discoveries when it is put in earth orbit in two years.
The next decades will truly be a rewarding time for Canadian astronomers and scientists.

ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-STATUS OF WOMEN Ms. Margaret Mitchell (Vancouver East) moved:
That this House condemns the Government for failing to recognize the real value of women's work in the workplace, the community and in the home with tangible policies that would ensure adequate incomes, removal of barriers and full opportunities for equal participation in decision making and in the political life of Canada.
She said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on behalf of the New Democratic Party today on the motion which indicates that we indeed condemn the Government for failing to recognize the real value of women's work in the workplace, in the community, and in the home. We feel that it should be recognized with tangible government policies, not just words, which would ensure adequate incomes, the removal of many barriers still remaining, and full opportunities for equal participation in decision-making and in the political life of Canada.
On Sunday, children young and old across Canada will celebrate Mother's Day to show their love and appreciation for the person who in most families still assumes major homemaking responsibilities as well as often works in the workplace and contributes in many ways to the community.
A few weeks ago we celebrated secretary's week. It was a week when bosses took their secretaries to lunch and often continued to pay low wages for the rest of the year.
Most women would agree that it is certainly nice to be loved and officially appreciated. We agree that this should be done not only once a year but on a year-round basis. It would be very nice if women had equal opportunities in all areas of their lives, including shared parental responsibilities and adequate income year-round.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has talked about equality quite frequently. Elis words look good on paper. We approve of the statement made at the First Ministers' Conference in Vancouver. We also approve of the appointment of two women judges. It was a major step forward.
However, most federal government policies-and it is policies which really count for women-lag far behind. While the policies and the legislation do not meet our expectations, I must say that the actions, the behaviour, and the attitudes of many Tory back-benchers are completely unacceptable. These days many of them seem to be scurrying about, extolling patriarchal values, eating illicit muffins, and trying through committees to move us backward in time as far as equality is concerned.
The Government has stated very strongly that it is for equality. Unfortunately it is being denied in the process. I have participated in two committees which have travelled across the country and spoken with women's groups. My sisters on the
Supply
other side of the House would agree that we want to be proud that all Members of Parliament are supporting equality and are trying to show appreciation to the many millions of Canadian women who have worked hard for equality over the past 15 years, and even before then. I am referring to the challenge which is under way regarding Secretary of State funding for women's programs. I will return to it later.
The New Democratic Party wants to pay tribute to millions of Canadian women who have worked long and hard to remove barriers for women. There are literally millions of them involved in different organizations across the country. They insist upon equality. Perhaps it is sometimes a little hard for a Government in power to take.
There will be a very strong lobby from the National Action Committee on the Status of Women on Monday. At least, I hope it will be very strong and well-informed as it always is. Women's groups like the NAC lobby constantly for legislative reform.
Women in the women's movement and organizations across the country, including organizations which have existed for many years, such as the Canadian Council of Women, give each other mutual support while they are working toward a change. Literally millions of Canadian women, as I said, are declaring that they will not go backward. They resent having to spend time and energy defending what they now have. They really resent reactionaries.
I know there are many Tory back-benchers who feel very strongly about equality, and I see some of them sitting in the House today. However, having been on two committees, I can tell the House that there are many who are not convinced and are actively working in the other direction.
I should now like to concentrate upon issues of concern to women who work in the workplace, in the home, and in the community. I remind Hon. Members very quickly, in the time available, of the barriers to equality that still exist about which we all know. In fact, in some areas they are increasing. We are concerned that we need effective, tangible government programs and policies to deal with the problems, to come to grips with the increasing and incredible poverty faced by women and the violence they are still facing despite all of us trying to work on the issue. They are faced with many inequalities, including very little participation in decisionmaking levels of all areas of life in Canada, but particularly in Government.
Very quickly on the economic situation for women, and I know my colleague will be commenting on this in more detail later, I regret to say that it is not improving. Let us have a look at the facts. First, let us consider the wage gap between men and women. Women's wages we know have been lower than men's for some time. It is appalling that the gap is increasing. In 1984, the average wage for women was 65.5 per cent of the average wage for men. Last year it was 64.9 per cent. It is

worsening. I was quite shocked to hear that in British Columbia, my province, women are earning 61.6 per cent of men's earnings. That is, women are earning 61-cent dollars, and yet there are so many of them, more than in any other province, who are raising families alone and who are in desperate poverty.
There is no question that we need much stronger equal pay for work of equal value, not only in the Public Service, the federal jurisdiction, but throughout society. We need enforcement of employment equity. We need pay equity legislation nationally as well as provincially.
Women continue to work primarily in low-paying job ghettos. The Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women has done studies on the Canadian Jobs Strategy programs and so has the Canadian Congress on Learning Opportunities for Women. In both studies it found that the Canadian Jobs Strategy is not helping to improve the situation for women. It is just reinforcing the trends that are there. Many of the training programs and job opportunities are in pink-collar jobs. Women are being directed to the low-paying job ghettos, even for re-entry programs. This is not improving the situation. We have to use government programs to open up new opportunities in non-traditional jobs and into jobs that are better paid, something that is not happening through the existing training programs.
We do not have effective affirmative action yet in our federal service. We must have a new look at the employment equity legislation from the point of view of making it mandatory. Women continue to be the major players in part-time jobs. Some people will say that that is fine because they have children and they just want to work part-time. Maybe that is the case sometimes but it is not all the time. There are many women who do not have much choice. Regardless of why they are part-time workers, they surely have the right to decent rates of pay, to benefits, to be able to pay into the Canada Pension Plan and so on. We asked the Minister responsible for the Status of Women, who I am glad to see in the House today, to look at the Canada Labour Code and to bring in reforms that will speed this up and help to cover prorated benefits for part-time workers, 70 per cent of whom are women.
We believe also that women's jobs are being threatened by certain government policies, certainly by privatization, often into non-union job categories by contracting out within groups like Canada Employment where we find more and more of this. As well I will include deregulation. There has not been protection for women. I hope there will be a serious in-depth study of the impact of these government policies.
In my question earlier today I mentioned that working parents have over 2.5 million children who need care. Workers who are parents, both men and women, need improved maternity and parental leave. Here again, I hope the Government, led by the Minister responsible for the Status of Women, will make sure that unemployment insurance coverage is improved to cover longer periods of benefits, certainly for maternity. Eventually over a number of years, we would like to allow maternity leave to 41 weeks with increased
benefits so that women and men, fathers and mothers, will have a choice during the first year of their child's life to be at home with the infant to help in its development and to enjoy that period. Most people who have to work are unable to do that, unless we have improved parental benefits. We are far behind European countries in that respect.
I want to spend a minute on child care. We know that this is absolutely critical for women in the workforce, for women in the home and for women working in the community in various roles. We need a very flexible, comprehensive, affordable and quality system of child care. That is why we want to have immediate action on the current crisis as well as long-term funding to ensure that children across the country and parents, particularly women, will have good quality child care and will not be worried about the kind of inadequate care or lack of care altogether with which they have to deal today.
I must say with all due respect that I hope the members of the Special Committee on Child Care were not reflecting government positions, but the Conservative Party has not fully accepted the current trends in families. We should not be spending time trying to go back to the old system of families. Changes have taken place. The majority of women are in the workforce and they will continue to be in the future. It is an irreversible trend; it is not positive or negative. It is up to every family to make its own decision. We should not be making people feel guilty. We should not be trying to look back to the past saying let us have incentives for women to stay in the home, to look after their husbands and to do the things that were perhaps a little more characteristic of a patriarchal family system.
If we are going to have adequate support for all workers in the workforce and for parents in the home raising children, we must have a national program for child care. We must have no further delays. We have to get on with an emergency plan right now and with the long-term planning that is under way with the provinces. The provinces will be unlikely to do very much unless there is considerable incentive from the federal Government with bucks to expand child care spaces.
Let me come to women's work in the home. Families are changing. I hope there are chances for more men to be in the home full-time who can consider this their vocation, at least for a certain period of their children's lives. As I say, we have to accept families as they are, not as they perhaps were in our generation or in our parent's generation.
Traditionally mothers have worked long hours as home managers, care givers and experts in many aspects of human relations. I do not think that home-makers and people who perform this very important role get enough recognition. They do not get enough recognition on job resumes when they go to look for a job. We should be making sure that this is recognized. They have very important skills. They have received no pay, little time off and they have no security for later years. Many women will be on their own for various reasons when they reach middle life. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, it is bad
May 8, 1987

enough for women pensioners but for women in their middle years who are left alone and who have not been in the workforce suffer tremendously. They are the quiet hidden poverty group in society.
Women in the home must be recognized for their work. The kind of token $200 per year per child refundable child tax credit proposed by the Special Committee on Child Care is more of an insult than a recognition. We need to have recognition of income levels to have a real choice. Of course, family incomes need to be adequate. We recommended a couple of years ago that the child tax credit be improved substantially and that it cover average income families as well. That would have been a much better way to go. The $400 million for this kind of token tax credit is not at all a good investment. I think most women realize this.
We also pushed hard, as did many women, to have family allowances reindexed as were old age pensions. Unfortunately, the Government did not listen to women and went ahead and deindexed family allowances. We need adequate pensions for all women. There should be adequate pensions for all workers, but particularly for women. Pensions are far from adequate at this time.
I believe it is unfortunate that rather than promoting equality in families, a number of people, including a number of Members of the House of Commons, are trying to promote the old traditional patriarchal family model. We all respect our forefathers and our foremothers, but today's families and young people are moving toward more shared parenting and toward options for both parents to be in the workforce as individuals and to have a chance to really enjoy their children and their home life.
I think it is the responsibility of government Members to lobby for equality, for equal opportunities and for forwardthinking policies. They should try to convince their colleagues that we do not want to go backward. We are going forward, not out of a lack of respect but because society has changed and will continue to change.
I was most disappointed that government members on the Special Committee on Child Care and; more recently, on the Secretary of State Committee looking into funding for women's programs seemed to want to go backward and were very reluctant to recognize the policy positions on equality their own Prime Minister put forward. This is not helping support of women's groups by the Government.
There are barriers for certain groups of women who are particularly disadvantaged, in fact doubly disadvantaged. I do not have a lot of time, but I want to mention single parents. The feminization of poverty continues to escalate and is most prevalent when a mother is left alone to care for children. Families headed by women are almost sure to be poor. After separation or divorce, the purchasing power of women is
Supply
reduced by 42 per cent while the purchasing power of men goes up by 70 per cent.
1 was very sorry to see the results of a study done by the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women. The advisory council studied three areas; areas in Ontario, Quebec, and B.C., and found that 10 per cent of all families in the Vancouver area are headed by women, most of whom have very low incomes. In the other two provinces, that figure is 8 per cent. Nationally, 60 per cent of all single-parent families headed by women live in poverty.
We would be willing to work with the Government on a major review of the situation of single-parent families. We should look at the entire question of the feminization of poverty and provide comprehensive programs to deal with that.
Many other women are doubly disadvantaged, including women who are battered, native women, immigrant women, women of colour, farm women and northern women. I wish I had time to comment further on them.
Finally, I want to talk about women in the community and in public life. Women contribute many millions of hours of quality time free to the community. We heard from a Quebec group, des Centres de Femmes Du Quebec, that the contribution of volunteer labour in women's centres alone is worth $2 million per year in that province.
We know that women are the ones who contribute to most of the community support services as home-makers, child care workers, librarians, school workers, hospital workers and workers in job-creation programs as well as in information and crisis centres. These women are all paid very low rates of pay. It is particularly disgusting what child care workers who are doing such an important job are paid. We must do much more about recognizing women's work in the community, both volunteer work and grossly underpaid work in essential community services.
I do not need to tell Members of the House of Commons that we are far from achieving equality in decision-making. A total of 38 women have been elected to sit in the House of Commons since 1921. On one occasion, Grace Maclnnis was the only woman Member of the House. At the current rate of increase, it will take 842 years before equal numbers of women and men are elected to Parliament.
I believe my female colleagues in the House will agree with me, that the recent First Ministers' meeting was symbolic of the lack of participation of women in the decision-making that affects Canada. There was not one woman present and I am sure it will be many years before a woman sits at that table and makes decisions on behalf of Canada.
1 mentioned some of the Government's policies which we feel do not go nearly far enough, and my colleagues will elaborate on that. We must deal with the problems of doubly disadvantaged women. We must look at the question of poverty and we must improve opportunities for women in all levels of society.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) called for the Government to recognize the real value of women who work in the home by providing tangible policies. She made two points in her speech. She said that women's work in the home must be recognized explicitly and that women who work in the home do not have security in their later years.
Will the Hon. Member work toward providing such explicit recognition by supporting changes in the Canada Pension Plan designed to recognize the real value of work done in the home by recognizing it as qualifying income for participation in the Canada Pension Plan? This would provide adequate security for women in retirement.

Mr Speaker, when 1 talk about explicit programs, I am not talking about women who are suffering from poverty now and cannot put an adequate amount of food on the table for their kids, waiting until, they are 65 before their problems are dealt with. That is a nice, comfortable rationale. People who do not deal with the present like to think that all we need to do is pat women on the head and ask their husbands to pay into a pension plan for them and maybe they will have something a bit better in the future.
We have a comprehensive policy to reform the Canada Pension Plan in order to bring women above the poverty line. Of course there must be major changes and there are different ways of doing this. We want to see what the Government will bring forward and we certainly want to recommend major changes for all women.
Most women are in and out of the workforce and do not have adequate coverage while in the workforce. If they drop out for seven years to have children, they should be building on their Canada Pension Plans during that time.
I would like to stress to my hon. colleague that we are talking about now, we have to deal with poverty and these intolerable inequities now. I really get tired of citing the statistics over and over again. We must deal with the real life situations of so many women who simply do not have adequate incomes today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
First of all, I think the Hon. Member is to be commended for again demonstrating her concern for the status of women.
However, it is too bad she decided to politicize the debate on such an important matter. Mr. Speaker, when the Hon. Member has given a clear and accurate explanation of the status of women in Canada and how it remains precarious despite all the efforts that have been made and the improvements that have taken place, it always surprises me that she always finishes her comments with a highly politicized statement. I say politicized because a partisan debate tends to ignore the progress that has been made and the very concrete and responsible action taken by this Government of which I am a Member.
I think we should consider that this Government has appointed six women as Ministers, a historic first, women like the Hon. Barbara McDougall, who have made their mark in the world, as they say, with policies like Bill C-42. I don't think we ever had a federal Act before that prohibited systematic discrimination against women.
How can the Hon. Member claim that the Government is to be condemned for failing to recognize the real value of women's work in the workplace?
Bill C-42 proves that this Government-both men and women-has recognized the importance of women in the workplace. And also in the home environment, because even if we expect every woman to be a Joan of Arc and to be active in our great causes, there are women who prefer to stay at home and raise their children. Why should these women be penalized financially just because they want to stay at home?
Our Government is bearing this in mind in its consideration of a daycare program. It wants to give women a real choice. If a woman wants to stay at home, she should not be penalized financially, and she should have access to the kind of daycare that meets her particular needs. On the other hand, if she wants to enter the labour market or if she has to enter the labour market for financial reasons, there again she should have access to the services she requires.
I wish the Hon. Member would consider the fact that women are not all the same, just as men are not all the same. We look at men as individuals, so why would she have us think that women all have the same needs? The only way to solve the problem of poor women is to spend money, but not by enrolling them in training courses nor forcing them to apply for traditional jobs. Again I ask the question: Why would she fail to admit that the Department of Employment and Immigration now have special programs specifically designed for women seeking employment in non-traditional fields? Why would she fail to acknowledge that the statistics released this morning indicate that 75 per cent of jobs created for women, men and young people are permanent, that the number of part-time jobs for women has declined, and that full-time jobs are on the increase? Indeed, we are making progress. Why would she deny that? Why would she deny that our Government is committed and that the status of women is not the exclusive bailiwick of the NDP? It no longer is.
Mr. Speaker, for someone who does not want politics to be political that was quite a speech.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: Those are facts.

I do not know quite where to start, except to say that we are hearing examples of wishful thinking. I know the Hon. Member wants to think that Bill C-42 really gets at the problems of women, but I would like her to show me where it has resulted in substantial improvement for women in either
May 8, 1987

job opportunities or pay equity. Equal pay for work of equal value must be stressed at all levels of society, and we can start with those jobs under federal jurisdiction. It is not now a part of our policies.
I would like to ask the Member to read again the report of the Special Committee on Child Care. In no way do the recommendations of the government majority give women an economic choice. How can you say that when 60 per cent of women in the workforce are there because they have to work? If both parents were not working they would be very poor. How can you say there is an option to remain at home? I am sure some of them would like to be at home while the children are very young, but how is it an economic choice to give them a refundable tax credit of $200 per child per year? That is no economic choice, that is an insult.
I am also curious to know why the Conservative Government is going to give that amount to Mila Mulroney or anyone else with a high income and the same amount to women on welfare when it is deducted from the welfare cheque? A refundable child tax credit is a very expensive way to go for very little benefit. Why not put that money into child care services which would be available for women in the home, men in the home, and parents in the workplace? I think that is most important.

speechtext: Resuming debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to join in this debate. It is most appropriate that it should start just prior to Mother's Day. I take this opportunity to congratulate all mothers, mothers in waiting, and grandmothers, of which I am one and about to be again. Today is a very special day.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext: Do aunts get a day, too?

Yes, absolutely, aunts and everyone else are going to have their day. Women are going to have their day.
It is important to acknowledge that there has been some significant improvement in the role of women since the late 1970s. That improvement needs to be treated with tender care so that it can grow and flourish. It only adds to the society in which we live when partners have an equal opportunity to work together to improve that society.
It would be a shame to expend the effort and energy to educate and train our daughters in the same way we train our sons, with equal pride in the attainments of both, to then not allow equal opportunity and equal choice to both, given equal competence.
Thank God for the differences between men and women and boys and girls. There are reasons why we need special policies to develop the kind of thinking that appreciates each other's role and each other's contribution to the growth and development of the society in which we live. That is the view of what I call the feminist of today, the people who recognize the ability
Supply
of women to contribute in equal measure at all levels of our society, all to the betterment of that society.
Women have had a very special role in creating that society. Unfortunately, it has not always been willingly, but rather often imposed and to the detriment of their growth, and therefore to the detriment of society as a whole. Nonetheless, it pays to keep this whole situation in historical perspective.
Women in Canada have played an important and influential role in the advancement of social justice, not just for women but for everyone. In Canada the movement for political suffrage was led by social feminists, sometimes called maternal feminists, who believed that women voters would force the Government to improve the quality of life for all Canadians. Attaining the vote was the first step in achieving those social goals.
Those women were appalled by the living conditions of low wage, low rent industrial workers, unschooled children, destitute widows, malnourished pregnant women, and child labour in the factories. It is not to say that men liked that situation; they just did not think along those lines. There was something wrong because the dynamics involved in having women at the legislative end were absent.
When women were enfranchised federally and provincially in the 1920s and 1930s in Canada, although as late as 1945 in Quebec, the statute books blossomed with a host of amendments and new legislation which alleviated old hardships, improved the lot of neglected children, destitute old people, deserted wives, indigent mothers of families, and the physically handicapped, as well as enlarging upon the grounds for divorce and support payments. They gave women the right to handle their own money and their own property.
It was a great indignity that we could do no banking of any significance without our husband's signature on the document. Most men accepted that indignity as a fact of life as if there was nothing wrong with it. There was something wrong with it. We were persons in our own right and had every right to act individually without the constraint of laws which were ineffective and uninterested in our well-being.
The new laws have protected women in industry and prohibited the outrageous exploitation of both male and female workers, especially young people. I will not give a history lesson, but there has certainly been great forward movement since the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. All political Parties can take credit for the forward movement of women's causes throughout the country.
In particular we should pay a special tribute to the women's lobby groups which have kept the women's agenda in the foreground. 1 was very honoured, as a past president of La Federation des femmes du Quebec, to represent that group of women in our affiliation with the National Action Committee, I'AFEAS, le Cercle de fermieres, the National Council of Women and the National Council of Jewish Women. I have

May 8, 1987
Supply
left many groups out. All these groups have been sensitive to and worked hard to put on public record the concerns of women as partners in society.
I am not extremely happy about the Tory record. All the right words have been used, all the right language is in place, and all the hyperbole is there. However, there is a lack of commitment in the form of action. Whether we talk about employment equity or employment in the workforce, the bottom line is economic independence and there are choices to be made in that regard. There needs to be some making up for the lack of equality which we have had.
Let us look at the structure of families today. We must not forget that 25 years ago most women did not work outside the home and had an average of four children. Today that structure has changed dramatically. The traditional family where children are living with their biological parents and the father is the sole breadwinner now accounts for less than one of six families.

Single wage earner families make up 29 per cent of all households. According to the November 1985 Statistics Canada figures, 57 per cent of women with pre-school children belong to the labour force. Sixty-seven per cent of gainfully employed women with small children hold full-time jobs, and the majority of women in their most reproductive years are on the labour market. In 1984, 69 per cent of women aged 25 to 34 were working. The different roles assumed by women in our society should be an incentive to implement a series of measures aimed at helping couples discharge their family responsibilities properly.
Among such initiatives, child care services are a priority. In that respect, I would point out that the Throne Speech recognized the need for child care, but instead of announcing specific measures, the Government simply decided to launch into vague discussions with provincial Governments, labour unions and private enterprise. A lot of talk, but little action.
Canadian men and women were expecting much more from this Government in the area of child care, because there is now a genuine crisis. Indeed, only 9 per cent of children who need them have places in child care services.
Mr. Speaker, the situation is totally unacceptable. Thousands of witnesses appeared before the Special Committee on Child Care and I toured British Columbia where I heard with my own ears parents complain they cannot find support services to enter the labour market, help their families, become income earners that can contribute something, improve their families' situation, and prevent them from falling into poverty. I for one find unacceptable that we are constantly awaiting action that is not forthcoming. In British Columbia, as elsewhere in Canada, we heard the same story.
Men and women across Canada expressed their disarray and problems caused by the tremendous difficulty they have finding child care places when they need to work or study.
What Canadians need and expect at this point is action rather than speeches.

Even prior to the Child Care Task Force which travelled across this land, with which I spent one week in the west, I travelled across the country on two occasions to participate in the Equality for All Task Force. I see a colleague in the House who participated on that task force and is well aware that one of the major concerns of the thousands of witnesses who appeared was the basic building block, represented by child care services, which includes a full range of services. It includes preschool children, part-time and full-time, evening hours, and, as well, the latch-key child up to the age of 14.
There are a variety of needs in this field because of the fact that women have a variety of needs. Women do not fit only one mold. They have a variety of reasons for going into the workforce, the most crying of which is to share with their partners the burden of meeting the budget needs of their families.
There is also the intellectual need of a woman who has had the opportunity of getting a proper education and wishes to have an enriched life by pursuing roles both outside and inside the home.
In addition, people have the right to make a choice. That right will be respected if we really believe in the right of equality for women.
The men and women who spoke to the task force on the need for child care were very eloquent, but we did not need a task force to learn what was needed. Our Party believes that the child care system must be based on the principles of sharing the burden and providing choices.

I would like to remind the House that out of 10 women-led single-parent families, six are living below the poverty line, as
May 8, 1987

opposed to most groups in society. The poverty rate has not declined among single mothers in 1985. In fact, in that group, poverty has been on a steady increase for five years. The odds for a single mother to join the have-nots are five times as high as for a married woman. Moreover, the wage gap between men and women widened in 1985, which made the headlines in all media not so long ago, on March 13. This is the first time in 18 years that women lost ground in their fight to reduce the salary gap between sexes, as indicated by Statistics Canada. I feel this is cause for concern, and we must look closer at that gap.
I think a great deal of it has to do with employment equity. The Government has often pointed to employment equity legislation as an example of concrete action which it has taken for the advancement of women. Yes, the language is good, as is the thought. All the groups that appeared before the committee when this legislation was being studied told us that Bill C-62 would be totally ineffective because it has no teeth. The goal of employment equity is to recognize the talents of individuals within the business community. This side of the House wishes to give equal opportunity to those who were discriminated against because of systemic barriers that need to be revised and reviewed.
I said that we have moved forward since 1975, but we have come to a standstill. This Bill and the need for employment equity was very obvious. I am sorry that there are no teeth in it so that we can really oblige companies to move forward.
I sit on the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture. We recently tabled in the House our recommendations for a new Broadcasting Act. We recommended that broadcasting licences include an obligation to establish an equal opportunity program in order to increase significantly the number of women and members of minority groups at all levels within each undertaking. Although data regarding the employment of minority groups in broadcasting are inadequate, we know that their members are found only too rarely in influential positions-as artists, journalists, managers and decision makers.
The broadcasting industry is already under the federal employment equity legislation. But the number of problems with that law as it is applied become very obvious when we look at broadcasting. This law applies only to employers with 100 or more employees. In the most crucial of industries where we can see ourselves on the screen and where we can see our
Supply
values reflected through the mirror of the little window box provided by the television, this Act is of no use in promoting the well-being of women and the portrayal of women. I will tell the Minister why I say that since I think it is serious.
On the basis of 1987 data obtained from the CRTC only 39 of 268 broadcasting corporations and only 15 cable companies out of the 360 existing cable companies in Canada have 100 or more employees. Thus there is no way that the Bill can be applied. That is the dilemma.
For the reasons I have just enunciated we have recommended that the new Broadcasting Act include provisions to increase significantly the number of women in minority groups, which includes women, at all levels of the broadcasting industry. If we want to be role models then we have to see ourselves somewhere. The present legislation breaks down in this regard and does not improve the inequities. Without an enforcement mechanism and a mandatory monitoring system we have a voluntary employment equity Act. I hope that the new Minister will look at this situation to find ways to make the legislation more effective.
I have said that Mediawatch and l'lnstitut Canadien de l'education aux adultes, ACTRA and many other groups that came before the committee asked us to address directly the need for the system to serve the needs of women, as well as men, and to reflect equitably their presence in the population.
In its presentation to our committee Mediawatch stated that men outnumber women two to one in prime time programming on public and private channels, and in children's programming four to one, although women account for over 50 per cent of the population. In addition to being under-represented they are performing a relatively limited number of stereotype roles. It is for these reasons that we want the broadcasting system to serve the interests and needs of both sexes. I certainly hope that the Minister will take this into consideration.
In conclusion, as we shape the forward agenda of the women's movement, and as we look at forward-looking strategies that we all worked on so hard and in which Canada was a true leader at Nairobi, it is important to note that there is no shortage of challenges left or of injustices to be resolved. We have come a long way, but we have not travelled the whole road yet. We need a special emphasis on those policy initiatives that allow and enhance the compatibility of family life and independence for women, that reaffirm the role of the family without abandoning the goals of feminism.
I will now give Hon. Members, from my point of view, a partial political action agenda for the rest of the decade. I think that we must change the attitudes of men and women so that true equality is established and allowed to grow. Attitudes in the media, in advertising stereotypes, in the soaps, in our workplaces and in our schools must also be changed.
Second, there must be changes to ensure employment equity through affirmative action and equal pay for work of equal value. I do not share the current Government's faith in its new employment equity legislation which fails to provide for

May 8, 1987
Supply
specific sanctions against employers who refuse to implement a program of employment equity in hiring practises.
Third, there needs to be media attention given to the plight of the poor, single women in our society, both single women as heads of families as well as the single elderly. Seven out of 10 spouseless women aged 70 and over are living in poverty in Canada. That is shameful. We must address, as well, the pension issue. Women work in the community and they work in their homes. They contribute thereby to the economy. We must find a way to acknowledge this so that they do not end up in a poor state in their later years. The value of the work performed, the home work that is performed, including house care, was calculated at 36 per cent of the Gross National Product in 1981 by Statistics Canada on a model that was developed in 1978.
Four, we need redoubled efforts to curb the violence against women and children that pervades our society. Women cannot be fully equal until incest, violent pornography, wife battering and other violence are dealt with, and dealt with sensibly and not radically.
Five, I think it is vital that the funding of women's groups continues, and continues at a level that will allow them to continue their role of advocacy in order to keep the barriers that we need to break down in front of the public eye, and certainly in front of the eyes of legislators. They need to be enabled to assure this equality among people.
Finally, I would like to use a term that is often feared around here, that is, choice in reproductive rights. Let us not be frightened off by this term. Reproductive rights include such issues as pregnancy leave, unemployment insurance benefits and the availability of child care. Child care is especially vital if women, particularly single mothers, are to gain economic independence. It should be apparent that women have an equal right to choose to work, which cannot be exercised in the best interests of their family or their children without providing accessible, affordable and adequate quality child care. No one here need be told how important good child care is to the attainment of women's and family rights.
I think I have presented a list of concerns. I hope that together all of us in this Flouse can meet the challenge for change. It is an ongoing process. We would be happy with the achievement of any one of them, but I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that women and women's groups will not rest until we have achieved every one of them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate my hon. friend for her very well documented speech and for her involvement in the promotion of women. I suggest that her personal life demonstrates that she is perfectly dedicated and that she assumes her duties beautifully. But I would like her to push her intellectual honesty a little further and recognize
what our Government has done to promote employment equity for women.
I am aware that my colleague who is responsible for the Status of Women will rise in a few minutes and make a very well documented speech, but I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) to recognize what our Government has accomplished.
Quite recently, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mrs. Vezina) refused to award a contract to a company which did not meet the criteria as far as employment equity for women is concerned. Her decision was almost a first! It had never happened before and it is something for which the Hon. Minister of Supply and Services should be commended.
In my riding, last week, on the first page of our daily newspaper, there was a picture showing the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) presenting a diploma or an award to a company, an Alcan subsidiary in my area, for recognizing the right to work and the participation of women in non-traditional trades, in this case, welding. And the company president said that his best welder was a woman.
All this to indicate that we are making progress indeed. We know that before we came into office only 10 per cent of women belonged to the Public Service. We are now up to 27 per cent. We know that we had two women ambassadors, we now have 21. I will let my colleague responsible for the status of women give more statistics in this field, but I should like to ask the Hon. Member for Ville Mount Royal whether she would agree that our Government has done a tremendous effort in this respect?

May I correct my colleague? I am not the Member for Ville Mount Royal, I am the Member for Mount Royal, which includes three cities. O.K. That is for openers.
Certainly I agree, and I think I was very clear about this issue for the benefit of my colleague. Still I would suggest that all Parties have promoted the cause of women. It is neither you nor us. I think that together, especially women MPs, we have made society aware of this and changed the mentality of our male colleagues here in the House. The Minister was able to recognize women's non-traditional work thanks to the women's movements who made this society aware of women's needs. During one of our World Wars, women proved they could be effective at non-traditional jobs, which means they have the capability and should have that choice throughout their years in the labour market. So the credit doesn't go to you as a Government or to us as a government. You have been able to promote the status of women thanks to women like Therese Casgrain and others, like the five women who helped define our position as persons in society, with equal rights and privileges. The movement started with them and has gone on to this day, and it will be thanks to historic developments and our own capabilities that we will finally get complete equality in our society. There are competent men and stupid men, and the same applies to women. But we should be treated equally in society. I am not here to praise the achievements of one
May 8, 1987

party over another. I am here to point out where you went wrong. I am here to suggest improvements. As far as the status of women is concerned, there are no partisan considerations. I think we should understand that together we will win this battle, and we will not win by going off in separate groups and deciding who is going to get money and who is not. It should go to the women who stood up for our cause and who were able to get us where we are today.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to hear the remarks of my colleague. I think all Hon. Members would agree that there are certainly no stupid women on any side of this House.
Hear, hear!

I am glad you agree. 1 know my colleague's commitment towards equality of women having worked with her on the Equality Rights Subcommittee and the report it brought forward. I think all Parties agree that this is not a particularly partisan issue in terms of the objectives we are trying to achieve. There are some differences, obviously, in the timing and some of the methods we use to achieve our goals, and I think in the debate today we will learn more about that from each other.
There is one thing which has really bothered me. In 1986 a study was done by the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women with regard to the aspirations of adolescent women. That study indicated, and do other reports as well, that today's teenage girls still see their lives in very traditional and romanticized terms, and are less likely than boys to make explicit plans for their future paid careers.
I am a mother of a 14 year old and in talking to her and her friends I think it is true that, no matter what we do in terms of moving forward on legislation and with different programs, if we somehow do not reach those young women they will not seek the kind of training and education they need and will end up in that sort of vicious cycle of poverty.
I wonder if my colleague has thought about this issue and if she could share with us any of her ideas as to how the federal Government and provincial Government agencies might deal with that very fundamental root problem in terms of working with women in the future?

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I had the pleasure of sharing many months and many hours of work with my hon. colleague who just raised the question. I would like to suggest that I think my friend and I looked at that question together. With another colleague I have also been looking at the impact on women through media. I think we will have the problem until such time as women start to feel a sense of their own worth and development and until they stop seeing themselves portrayed on probably the most powerful medium in our society today, television, in those kinds of sex stereotyping stories we see on the television screen, whether through advertising or the programs which are shown. That medium must start to change and give value and importance to
Supply
education, post-secondary education, and show women as full partners having intelligent, equal conversations with their partners.
I think as well that schools should start to develop a curriculum which does not say, "Jane goes out to buy the oranges while John goes to buy the tools in the hardware store". If it could have Jane and John doing the opposite occasionally, the stereotypes could be broken.
It is a long hard row. We have been ingrained but, I hope not restrained, from some creative action. I would like to tell my colleague that I have an 11-year old granddaughter and she is not interested in the stereotype world. I suppose it has something to do with family upbringing and role models. I would prefer to have debates of this kind and not have the kind of partisan elements I have occasionally listened to in this House.
I could give my hon. friend a long list of the accomplishments of those on this side of the House, starting way back with Judy LaMarsh and forward, and my hon. friend could start with Ellen Fairclough and others, but that would not change the situation and the daily living for women in today's society and prepare them for tomorrow. Let us try to keep this on the level which I think will be helpful to the forward movement of women in today's society.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend and colleague stated that reproductive rights were basic to equality and defined reproductive rights in very broad terms. I agree with her on that, but she did not mention the whole question of choice in relation to access to abortion.
Last month a pregnant 14-year old girl was refused an abortion in a Kamloops hospital. As a result she had to go through a very prolonged forced premature delivery, which I am sure will create tremendous trauma for her for the rest of her life.
Does the Hon. Member have any suggestions about what she feels should be done on the whole question of access under our existing law? Also, what should be done about more effective preventive measures including better contraception so that women really have reproductive rights?

Mr. Speaker, in a sense I am glad the Hon. Member has asked the question, although I could have done without it. I am pleased to share my point of view.
Those of us who travelled with the Equality for All task force were faced with the question of the right to choice versus the right to life. We heard the hard core views on both sides, and there does not seem to be, in society today, the kind of atmosphere which would enable us to make the choice on one side or the other by opening up the legislation.
It has been my view that a woman has the right to make the choice for herself after having received the best counselling and the best advice possible, after all the options have been

May 8, 1987
Supply
made available to her and there is an understanding of all the options, including adoption and the kind of support the state can give a woman who chooses to keep the child herself. If all those support systems are in place-and I will come to the Hon. Member's case in a moment-and if we had the proper kind of education and training to teach respect for one's self and taking responsibility for one's actions, I would say to the Hon. Member that it would not be the kind of problem it is today.
1 do not think we can open up the abortion question in today's society. I think we will have to work with what exists in our law presently and apply it in an intelligent way. It will take government will at the provincial level, because that is where health services are determined, to find the answer to how to allow a woman to make her own choice in reproductive rights.
In respect of the case of the 14-year old child, as a director of youth protection I faced much younger children than that, such as a 7-year old and a 13-year old who were pregnant by incest and by rape. Anyone who tells me that we should have the kind of society which does not allow for the humane determination of termination in that instance is out of his or her mind, in my view. First, the child's body has not developed healthfully enough for her to sustain and give a healthy body to the foetus. Second, I do not believe that any family would want to impose that on a child.
In respect of the Hon. Member's question, I hope I have elucidated clearly enough that I would not reopen the issue in the Criminal Code at this point.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to rise in my place today to discuss the issue because it is a very important one to all of us in Canada. Perhaps what has been missing so far in the debate is that it is important to men as well as to women. Within society we have come a long way over many years, as the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) pointed out.
I guess in the beginning women were fighting alone for things which they felt were important for themselves and things they felt were important for society. It gives me great pleasure-and it gives the women in this Party great pleasure-that we now have so many men as our allies. Let us make no mistake about the fact that women, not men, have put the issues of child care, the elderly poor, and so on, on the agenda. Women should take credit for it. Let them also remember that there are many people on their side. As we move forward from here, as we must continue to do and are doing, that is an important building block for how we approach women's issues in the future.
While I am very happy to debate the issue, I am very surprised by the wording of the motion. The fact is that the Government has put in place a number of programs for action on women's issues. The Government's whole strategy contains a comprehensive and pragmatic series of initiatives, I may say among the best ever introduced in Canada.
Let us look at what our achievements have been in 2.5 years. There has been reform of Canada's divorce laws and family enforcement orders, a very important element which women have needed for many years. There has been a repeal of the Indian Act provisions which discriminated against native women for decades. We introduced the first employment equity legislation ever introduced in Canada, opening up a full range of labour market opportunities for women.

The implementation of a National Training and Employment Program which, for the first time, defines participation goals for women, proposes steps to increase the number of pension beneficiaries and makes them more equitable, and the passage of legislation to put an end to the sexual exploitation and the sexual abuse of children.
As suggested by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), Mr. Speaker, our Government has given top priority to women's concerns. A document entitled Dimensions of Equality: A Federal Government Work Plan for Women clearly demonstrates our commitment to women's concerns. Tabled in November of last year by the Prime Minister at the yearly Conference of the First Ministers in Vancouver, this document describes our Government's biannual action plan to promote women.

Let me say that the document contains a number of measures. Earlier I pointed out the legislation surrounding divorce and family enforcement orders. Let me point out, in terms of progress for women, that not one of these issues is a new one. These issues have been around, and women have been asking about them for years. We have made an incredibly good start in the first half of our mandate, and we are not finished yet. That is what this book outlines.
Less than six months after its tabling, a number of the initiatives have already been accomplished or are well under way. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) announced that the Canadian Forces would conduct trials with women in combat. A review of sex stereotyping in internal government communications is nearing completion, further to the review of external communications which was completed last year.
Let me just say about the problem of stereotypes that in the earlier Bill introduced on communications there was forward momentum to deal with the problem of sex stereotyping. We all know how important it is to develop, not just role models for children but their own attitudes toward themselves. This will be very important to the women of the future.
Labour Canada conducted an educational seminar for labour representatives on equal pay for work of equal value. The Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) funded a national conference which was held in Toronto as a follow-up to the 1985 Nairobi forum and the United Nations World Conference on Women, as well as a successful national conference on immigrant women and visible minority women.
May 8, 1987
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext:
Let me say as well that we have met with representatives of groups to discuss very specific issues and we will be meeting again with the NAC executive and many of its members on Monday. Many of our members will be there. Complementing this process, a dialogue, of course, has been our determination to bring more women into positions of power and influence.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) talked about this participation of women in roles of leadership and in politics.

During the 1984 election campaign, we had promised, if elected, to increase from 15 per cent to 30 per cent the rate of representation of women in federal agencies, boards and commissions. Only halfway through our mandate, the rate is now 27 per cent. It is only a beginning, but it is quite significant. Deputy Ministers and Assistant Deputy Ministers occupy also key positions in the Public Service. When we came to power, there were only three women appointed at that high level. There are now nine, including the Chairman of the Public Service Commission, as well as the Deputy Minister of Labour, the Deputy Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Deputy Minister of Supply and Services, and the Deputy Minister of Privatization. The incumbents of these positions of trust can make key contributions and may even further the economic and social advancement of all women.

I mentioned earlier that the Canadian Forces will be undertaking trials with women in combat. Let me mention as

May 8, 1987
Supply
well that my colleague, the Minister of National Defence, has appointed Canada's first woman general, Brigadier-General Sheila Hellstrom. The number of positions in the Armed Forces open to women has risen from 19 per cent in 1971 to 75 per cent today.
Two eminent women now head the Economic Council of Canada and the National Capital Commission. Recently two women were appointed to the Board of Directors of the Bank of Canada. Other government agencies now have numerous women. There are now 10 women occupying senior diplomatic posts as ambassadors and consuls general. Of the 12 people the Prime Minister appointed to the other place, four are women.
In addition to a 22 per cent increase in the number of federally appointed women judges, let me point out and publicly congratulate, Madam Justice Claire L'Heureux-Dube on her appointment to the Supreme Court of Canada. What this tells us is not that women are getting appointed, but that they are being appointed to the highest and most influential positions in the land.
This is one indication of what we are doing. It is important, and I have pointed this out in this House before, first, because it is a legitimate recognition of the contribution that women have made-finally a recognition of their contribution and their talents. Also, it is important because when men and women sit down at the same table to work toward a common objective then the old stereotypes start to change and fall away along with the old attitudes.
As the Prime Minister said, our aim is to improve and perfect our democratic way of life. If we wish to correct the imbalance which still exists, we must increase further the presence of women in the national decision-making process.
Let us go back to women and their political role. There were only two women Cabinet Ministers in the last Government. There are now five, and I say with all due modesty that I think we do our share. I know this has been of great concern to the other Parties. I think particularly of a Member of the Liberal Party, a former president, who talked about the invisible ceiling for women, a glass ceiling where women can only reach so far and cannot go beyond it. Let me describe where 1 think women are in our Party.
Women for a long time did face a lot of barriers. They continue to face some. There was a big brick wall; then women started punching out some of those bricks. Enough holes are now in that wall so that it is going to start to fall down. That is the difference in how this Party views the role of women and how the former Government viewed the role of women. We are not only hopeful but we are going to help women get to where they should be.
Let me say, on employment equity, how important this Bill is. The Hon. Member for Mount Royal pointed out that it was not working, and I think the Hon. Member for Vancouver East said the same thing, that employment equity should be mandatory, that there should be quotas on things to regulate every move that business makes.
I have been monitoring this very closely and talking to people in human resources in the private sector who are inundated with requests from businesses and financial institutions anxious to meet the requirements of this Bill. The old stereotypes are changing. Business now knows that it is in its interest that women have an equal opportunity. The future of business will have to embrace the resources represented by women in society.
The number of people who are of an age to leave school is declining very rapidly. In order for business, commerce and universities to be competitive and productive in the future, they will have to draw on a wider range of talent and that includes women. They are starting to recognize that. If we can embrace them in a partnership without simply having the Government making rules, then women will be much better off.
There is a traditional women-as-victims attitude. Yes, women have problems that men to do not have, there is no question about that. However, one cannot transfer what was once a hope and faith in Prince Charming to a hope and faith in the Government. Women are better than that. Women contribute; women have talent; women make their own decisions; women can hold their heads up high along with all the men in Canada, and women working together with men can also help those women who are not in a position to do so.
Our objective is to have men and women start equally. Sometimes men start higher than women so in order for women to start equally we have to help. That does not mean that once women get there they are not every bit as able to contribute as are men. We recognize that.
Let me deal with the poverty statistics for a moment. Between 1982 and 1984, the number of women over age 16 living in households below the National Council of Welfare's poverty line rose by 118,000. This is a matter of real concern to everyone and every political Party. The proportion of women over 16 living in poverty rose from 17.3 per cent to 18.5 per cent, and that occurred during part of the economic recovery. That is serious.
Between 1984 and 1985, the number of women over 16 living in poverty dropped by 69,000. We were able to bring that figure back down to where it started. That is not anywhere like good enough, but we are glad to see that happening. We have given it a nudge in the right direction because of some of the things we have introduced.
Obviously jobs relate directly to poverty. During the first 30 months of this Government's term of office, the number of women with jobs rose by 406,000. During the last 30 months of the previous Government's term, the number of women with jobs throughout the entire period of recovery rose by only 250,000. The difference of 156,000 is greater than the total number of people employed in the whole of Metropolitan London, Ontario, a fine metropolis.
May 8, 1987

The contrast in the increase in full-time jobs for women between the two periods is even more striking. During the last 30 months of the former Liberal Government's term, the number of women with full-time jobs rose by 128,000 and during the first 30 months of this Government's term, the increase was 327,000, a difference of 199,000 or over two and a half times as many.
It is important that women now have benefits in part-time jobs, that they have benefits in full-time jobs and that they get more full-time jobs. That is why the training programs we introduced have been so important. That is why the child tax credit and the sales tax credit were so important. They helped to move women out of poverty and into more comfortable and prosperous lives. We must all focus on that, particularly for elderly women, and that is why we have introduced so much pension legislation. We know how important that is.
That is the record of the Government in two and a half years. That is why I believe this motion is frivolous and should be defeated.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know how the Minister responsible for the status of women could call this a frivolous motion. It is a very serious motion, and I hope she knows me and my Party well enough to realize that it was put in all seriousness.
I would like to ask the Minister a question about the Secretary of State women's program which, as she knows, has been in some turmoil of late. I would like to know her view of the purpose of this program and why we have had to spend so much time, money and hours on the road with the SOS Committee defending this program when it is very obvious that the program is essential to carrying out the equality goals of the Government. Does she support the views of some Conservative Members on the committee who have been very difficult, members who have suggested that advocacy groups should not receive government funding, that groups like NAC should not be funded if REAL Women is not eligible for funding?
Second, the Minister mentioned the child care program. What is her position on the recommendation of the special committee on child care regarding the refundable child tax credit which would cost about $300 million and put $200 in the hands of each woman with young children? Would this money not be better spent by increasing child care spaces and improving the quality and flexibility-and I agree with her on that point-of child care across Canada?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe the Hon. Member was not quite listening. I did not in any way suggest that she was frivolous or that the issue was frivolous. I said that the motion was frivolous.
If we are to engage in a discussion about women, we have to recognize and celebrate together some of the positive things that have happened. It is a case of whether the glass is half full or half empty. Until the glass is completely full, I would like to
Supply
talk about it in a positive way. Compared to what has gone before, the progress that has been made is something with which I can certainly face the country very happily.
I believe the women's program has made an important contribution to the ability of women to articulate the things about which they care. Like any program, it is worth reviewing from time to time. We should hear what Canadians think of the program, if the program is working and if needs have changed in the last five or 10 years. The inquiry that is being conducted both by the Secretary of State and by the House of Commons is a perfectly legitimate one. Having said that, I would certainly think it is quite worth while to continue funding some kinds of advocacy programs and I do not in any way disagree with that.
I do believe that there must be some criteria and perhaps it is time the criteria for our objectives changed. I have made no prejudgement on that. I would like to see what comes out of the House of Commons committee's study and the review of the Secretary of State. I would like to see more services for women and not just a continuation of some women's programs.
Once again, we need flexibility in child care. The report of the special committee was a very thoughtful one and attempted to deal with flexibility and the many different ways women need help in looking after children. I agree with the Hon. Member that the definition of family has changed. That means that we should do something for women who want to care for their children at home and something for women who need a structured system. We are taking that into account as we develop government policy because we all know what the options are. They are to fund the supply side, which is additional space, or fund the demand side, which is to give parents money directly. We all have a different view of where to draw the line between the one and the other.
I think the Special Committee on Child Care is to be commended for the work it did and the report it presented. I know this is an issue that the Hon. Member cares about as well. The fact that there is ongoing discussion with the provinces, and the report will be a part of that discussion, means that by the time we come forward with a policy it will be positive and will help the women of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is an easy question to answer because the answer is obviously yes. What is not clear to me from the Hon. Member's comments is what is the proportion of SMs that took the course and so on. It is not just the number that is significant but the proportion at each level.
